payload.text: A peat bog looks like waste ground, and for centuries that is exactly how it was {{b1}}. Drained, cut and burned, it gave farmers a field and households a cheap fuel. What nobody counted was the carbon: waterlogged moss decays so slowly that a metre of peat may hold the remains of a thousand years of plants, and the bogs of the world store more carbon than all its {{b2}} put together. Once the water table drops, that store begins to leak into the air. Restoration is unglamorous work, mostly blocking ditches and letting the ground go {{b3}} again, but it is far cheaper than planting the trees that would be needed to {{b4}} the same amount.

payload.text: Speaking two languages does not make anyone cleverer, whatever proud parents may {{b1}}. What it does is give the brain constant practice at one narrow skill: choosing a single system while holding the other one back. Both languages stay switched on, so every sentence obliges the speaker to {{b2}} the words that do not belong. Psychologists find that bilinguals are quicker at tasks with a similar shape, such as ignoring a distraction or changing rule in the middle of a game, and slower, by a fraction of a second, at simply {{b3}} everyday objects. The advantage, in other words, is not general intelligence but a very well-trained {{b4}}.

payload.text: A volcano rarely erupts without warning; the difficulty is that the warnings are written in signals nobody can feel. Weeks beforehand, magma pushing upwards makes the ground {{b1}} by a few centimetres, small earthquakes multiply, and the gases leaking from the summit change their mixture. Satellites and instruments on the slope now record all three, and in several countries the readings are streamed to the public rather than kept in a laboratory. The remaining problem is human. An alert issued too early empties a town for nothing and makes the next warning easier to {{b2}}, while an alert issued too late is worthless. Officials therefore speak in levels of {{b3}} rather than in dates, and ask people to prepare for something that may never {{b4}}.

payload.title: The Town That Aimed Its Lights Downwards
paragraphs: Flagstaff, in northern Arizona, has been fussy about its lighting since 1958, when the city banned searchlights to protect the work of an observatory on the hill above it. What began as a favour to astronomers has hardened into an unusually detailed code: street lamps must throw their light downwards, the brightness of shop signs is capped, and most of the town is lit by lamps whose colour sits at the warm end of the spectrum. Visitors often arrive expecting a dim place. It is not dim; it is simply lit where the light is wanted.

The argument for copying Flagstaff has quietly moved away from astronomy. Ecologists have spent two decades documenting what a lit night does to animals that evolved without one: moths circling a lamp until they drop, hatchling turtles crawling inland towards a car park instead of the sea, migrating birds pulled into cities and killed against glass. Blue-rich white light, the kind that arrived with the switch to LEDs, is the worst offender, and that switch was made almost everywhere on the grounds that it would save electricity.

The saving is real but smaller than promised, because cheap light invites more of it; towns that changed their bulbs frequently ended up lighting streets that had never been lit before. The remedy is not darkness, which nobody is proposing, but discipline about direction, colour and hour. Where councils have tried it, dimming after midnight, shielding fittings and choosing amber over blue, complaints have been rare and bills have fallen, which suggests that the obstacle was never public opinion.

questions.prompt: 本文の主旨として最も適切なものはどれですか。

LEDs should be abandoned altogether, because every town that installed them has seen its electricity bills rise.
Light pollution is essentially a problem for astronomers, so towns without an observatory have little reason to change their lighting.
Public opposition is the main reason councils have been unable to reduce street lighting after midnight.

payload.title: The Language That Came Back
paragraphs: When the last speaker who had grown up with Manx died in 1974, the language was written up as a closed case, and international lists duly recorded it as extinct. The obituary was premature. Enthusiasts had been recording the old speakers on tape since the 1940s, and a smaller group had learned to speak from those recordings: imperfectly, with English vowels, but well enough to argue about grammar in a pub.

The revival became serious only when it stopped being an adult hobby. In 2001 a primary school opened on the island in which every subject is taught in Manx, and the children who passed through it now supply most of the language’s young speakers. Purists complained, reasonably enough, that the Manx coming out of the classroom was not the Manx of the tapes: the idioms were thinner, and the sentence patterns leaned towards English.

What a school cannot manufacture is a reason to use the language outside it. Manx has perhaps two thousand people with some ability in it and a few dozen households raising children in it, which is enough for songs, road signs and a weekly radio slot, and nowhere near enough for a labour market. Its defenders have therefore stopped promising restoration and now describe a smaller, harder goal: making sure that in every generation somebody grows up with the language.

questions.prompt: 本文の主旨として最も適切なものはどれですか。
options: Manx survived through tape recordings and a school that produced new young speakers, but the language that returned differs from the old one and still has few everyday uses, so its supporters now aim only at continuity between generations.
Manx died out in 1974, and the attempt to teach it in schools has failed to produce any new speakers at all.
The chief obstacle to reviving Manx has been the refusal of purists to accept any change in its grammar.
Manx is now used widely enough on the island to support employment and ordinary business in the language.

questions.before: The revival gained real momentum once
questions.after: instead of remaining something that adults studied in their spare time.

questions.sentence: Fluency, it turns out, is easier to arrange than a reason to use it.

questions.prompt: 筆者が本文全体で最も伝えたいことはどれですか。
options: A language can be recovered from recordings and passed to children, but the version that comes back is altered, and it lasts only if each generation is deliberately given it.
